findings.headline: Your stop-payment fee is an extreme outlier.
findings.body: At $43.00, your stop-payment fee is more than double the $20 median of 66 comparable credit unions — the 98th percentile, flagged as an extreme outlier. Three quarters of your peers charge $30 or less. This is a service fee members request in moments of stress, which makes an outlier price here disproportionately visible.

findings.headline: Two more fees sit at the very top of the cohort.
findings.body: Deposited-item returns run $40.00 against a $20.00 median — the highest value among 25 peers — and paper statements run $5.00 against a $2.75 median, at the top of 28 peers. Add an NSF fee of $30 versus a $25 median (83rd percentile), and your penalty-and-exception stack occupies the cohort's ceiling across multiple lines.

findings.headline: Your everyday fees are genuinely member-friendly — and unknown.
findings.body: Card replacement ($3.00 vs a $25.00 median, 11th percentile across 94 peers), monthly maintenance ($1.00 vs $3.50, 39th percentile), and cashier's checks ($2.00 vs $4.00, 31st percentile) all price well below comparable credit unions. The schedule's generous half is real; it simply earns nothing today because nobody has been told about it.

exec_narrative: Net position: Coopers Cave runs a barbell schedule. Exception and penalty fees sit at or near the top of the cohort — a stop-payment fee flagged as an extreme outlier, deposited-item returns and paper statements at the cohort maximum, NSF above a falling median — while everyday service fees like card replacement and monthly maintenance price near the bottom. Three categories (overdraft, overdraft-protection transfer, incoming domestic wire) are absent from the published schedule. The barbell is the risk: members and reviewers notice the ceiling fees, and the generous floor earns no offsetting credit. The three findings above are the agenda for a one-hour pricing conversation.

callouts.title: Stop payment — $43.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $20.00 · P75 $30.00 · 98th percentile · n=66 · flagged: extreme outlier (>2x median)
callouts.body: At more than double the peer median, this is the single most conspicuous line on your schedule. Stop payments are requested by members already dealing with a problem — a lost check, a disputed payment — so the fee lands at a moment of maximum sensitivity. Whether the answer is a cut toward the $20 center or a documented rationale, this fee should be a decision rather than an inheritance.

callouts.title: Deposited item return — $40.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $20.00 · peer max $40.00 · 100th percentile · n=25
callouts.body: You hold the cohort ceiling on a fee that charges members because someone else's check failed — a charge members consistently experience as unfair, since the failure is not theirs. Fees that penalize members for third-party behavior are exactly the category regulators and comparison surveys highlight first. At double the median, this line pairs with the stop-payment outlier to define your schedule's exposure.

callouts.title: NSF / returned item — $30.00
callouts.body: The industry-wide retreat from NSF fees has reached small credit unions: your cohort's median is $25 and the low end has already reached zero. A $30 fee is not yet an outlier, but it sits on the wrong side of a falling trend line and compounds the top-of-cohort posture established by your other exception fees.

callouts.title: Everyday fees — near the bottom of the cohort, marketed nowhere
callouts.stat: Card replacement $3.00 vs $25.00 median (P11) · Monthly maintenance $1.00 vs $3.50 median (P39) · Cashier's check $2.00 vs $4.00 median (P31)
callouts.body: Three routine member fees price at a fraction of the cohort. If deliberate, they are the foundation of a member-value story your peers' own published schedules substantiate — one that could offset the exception-fee optics above. If not deliberate, they are margin available without touching a headline fee. Below market and invisible is the one position that earns nothing.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF and penalty pricing generally: the largest institutions have eliminated returned-item fees, regulatory attention to so-called junk fees has intensified, and the pressure now reaches small credit unions — visible in your own cohort, where a quarter of peers price NSF at $20 or less. Second, published fee schedules have become public documents in practice: scraped, compared, and surfaced in searches, which converts every top-of-cohort line into a small reputational bet.

Small community credit unions compete on relationship and trust, which makes fee coherence unusually valuable at your scale — members forgive a fee they understand and resent one that feels arbitrary, and a $43 stop payment next to a $1 maintenance fee reads as arbitrary. The highest-leverage moves here are surgical: bring the two or three ceiling fees toward the cohort center, publish the categories currently missing from the schedule, and start telling the genuinely member-friendly story the bottom half of your schedule already contains.
